title: Testing Adaptive Friction for Generative AI Programming Through Reproducible Simulations
abstract: Generative AI can accelerate programming while leaving independent competence insufficiently tested. This study develops a joint decision rule requiring adaptive reasoning prompts to demonstrate a meaningful transfer gain without excessive completion time. A reproducible simulation compared ordinary assistance, static friction, and adaptive friction using a continuous ability moderator and correlated learning and time outcomes. Six scenarios were evaluated at three sample sizes, with 5,000 replications per configuration. In one illustrative dataset of 165 synthetic users, adaptive friction increased the transfer index by 7.53 points and produced a geometric time ratio of 1.023 relative to ordinary assistance. These quantities reflect imposed assumptions, not observed human effects. Across repeated favourable simulations, the joint criterion passed in 54.2%, 87.0%, and 99.1% of runs at sample sizes of 165, 330, and 660. A separate detector model showed how false prompts can breach the time budget despite preserving expected learning gains. The contribution is an auditable evaluation framework connecting meaningful benefit, efficiency limits, and trigger uncertainty. Prospective human studies remain necessary to establish effectiveness.
introduction: Generative artificial intelligence changes the cost of producing plausible solutions, but a completed task does not reveal how much its author understands. Experiments on professional writing and workplace support document productivity gains under particular conditions [@noy;@brynj]. Such evidence makes assisted programming attractive to educators and employers, while leaving a separate question unresolved: what remains when assistance disappears? Research in mathematics education demonstrates that interface safeguards can alter the relationship between assisted performance and subsequent unaided achievement [@bastani]. Programming evaluation therefore needs to distinguish productive collaboration from the temporary substitution of machine output for human competence.

Cognitive offloading provides a more precise starting point than claims that AI inevitably damages thinking. External resources redistribute processing demands [@risko], and expectations of later access can change what people remember [@sparrow]. Neither mechanism establishes inevitable deterioration. The relevant design problem is whether delegation supports learning, displaces essential practice, or does both across different users and tasks. Work on automation distinguishes appropriate use from misuse and disuse [@paras]. Trust consequently matters when it tracks system capabilities and contextual demands [@lee]. A high acceptance rate, rapid insertion, or unchanged code block cannot independently diagnose careless reliance.

Reasoning prompts offer one plausible intervention. Self-explanation research links explanation generation to understanding [@chi], retrieval practice can improve later retention [@roediger], and broader learning research cautions that instructional techniques differ in effectiveness and generalisability [@dunlosky]. Nevertheless, additional interaction is not automatically educational. Cognitive load [@sweller] and expertise reversal [@kalyuga] make indiscriminate prompting questionable, particularly when experienced programmers already understand a recommendation. Cognitive forcing functions have also been investigated directly in AI-assisted decisions [@bucinca]. Adaptive friction therefore cannot credibly be introduced as the first attempt to interrupt unreflective AI use. Its value depends on selecting useful occasions without imposing disproportionate interruption costs.

Human–AI interaction guidelines emphasise intelligibility, correction, and user control [@amershi]. Studies of explanations and appropriate reliance further show why confidence, acceptance, and decision quality require distinct measurements [@lai;@schemmer]. Related supplied work addresses trust calibration across organisational settings [@s40] and institutional AI governance [@s68]. A surgical-training preprint proposes evaluating competence after feedback withdrawal [@s32], while an education preprint considers pedagogical uncertainty and belonging [@s84]. These sources motivate attention to agency and independent performance; they do not identify the causal effect of adaptive prompts in programming. Transfer across domains remains a hypothesis requiring direct investigation.

The methodological opportunity is to connect interface evaluation to an explicit decision standard. Demonstrating any positive mean effect is weaker than demonstrating a worthwhile benefit within an acceptable time budget. Equivalence testing separates negligible differences from statistically inconclusive comparisons [@schuirmann;@lakens]. Joint requirements are especially relevant when productivity gains could otherwise compensate numerically for unacceptable learning loss. Adaptive-intervention research supplies complementary concepts for defining decision occasions [@nahum] and identifying proximal effects through repeated randomisation [@klasnja]. Here, those concepts inform a future experimental programme rather than implying that a working adaptive interface has already been validated.

The policy also requires a definition of independent competence. Debugging an unfamiliar implementation, explaining a boundary condition, and applying a concept to a new problem measure different capabilities. Prompt acceptance and self-reported confidence can supplement these assessments but cannot replace them. This separation prevents interface telemetry from simultaneously defining the intervention trigger and serving as circular evidence that the intervention improved reasoning.

This article develops a simulation-based evaluation of that decision problem, following principles for transparent simulation design [@morris]. Its contribution is threefold: a noncompensatory learning-and-time criterion, an operating-characteristic analysis under favourable and unfavourable assumptions, and an analytical account of trigger sensitivity and specificity. The research questions concern how often a candidate policy satisfies both requirements, whether the proposed sample size detects ability moderation, and how inaccurate triggers change expected feasibility. The supplied experimental blueprint establishes the starting assumptions, not empirical evidence. All supplied bibliographic records are retained in an applicability assessment, with unresolved metadata distinguished from checked sources. The resulting framework supports a defensible trial design while deliberately withholding claims about demonstrated human learning gains.
methodology: We conducted a computational design study, not a participant experiment. Three equally sized synthetic arms represented ordinary assistance, fixed reasoning prompts, and adaptive prompts. Baseline ability followed a standard normal distribution and remained continuous. The illustrative dataset used 55 units per arm. Table 1 specifies assumed coefficients; no parameter was estimated from human observations. Transfer was modelled as a continuous index in point units rather than a bounded test proportion. The bivariate model was:

In (1), the design vector contains an intercept, static and adaptive indicators, ability, and both treatment–ability interactions. The coefficient vectors govern immediate transfer and log completion time. Residual standard deviations were 6.5 points and 0.12 log minutes, with correlation 0.30. Separate ordinary least-squares fits produced conditional contrasts at mean ability and Student confidence intervals. Delayed outcomes were secondary illustrations generated by (2), with arm-specific decrements and independent Gaussian noise of standard deviation four.

The primary policy decision required the one-sided 95% lower confidence bound for adaptive transfer benefit to exceed five points and the corresponding upper bound for its geometric time ratio to remain below 1.10. Equation (3) defines this intersection–union rule. Both thresholds are illustrative design choices requiring stakeholder justification. Time non-inferiority uses only the upper bound; descriptive equivalence additionally requires a 90% interval within [0.90, 1.10]. The exact log limits are log(0.90) and log(1.10), which are asymmetric.

We evaluated six mechanisms at total sample sizes 165, 330, and 660, with 5,000 independent replications per configuration. Scenarios varied adaptive benefit, moderation, and time cost while retaining the static comparator. Outputs included superiority rejection, time non-inferiority, joint passage, interaction rejection, bias, and interval coverage. Monte Carlo standard errors quantified simulation precision. The intersection–union decision concerns one prespecified policy; additional confirmatory comparisons would require a declared family and multiplicity control [@holm].

Equation (4) separately examines expected detector feasibility using prevalence, sensitivity, specificity, prompt benefit, false-prompt harm, and aggregate interruption cost. It is an analytical sensitivity model, not a fitted explanation of the arm-level simulation. All simulations used complete outcomes. A future randomised trial should retain all allocated participants, record reasons for missingness, and prespecify imputation and departures from missing-at-random assumptions [@rubin;@mice]. No missing-data test can establish those assumptions. Code, generated data, coefficients, and random seeds accompany the manuscript.

In (4), p is need prevalence, s sensitivity, c specificity, b benefit when a needed prompt is delivered, h harm from an unnecessary prompt, k total added minutes if every eligible occasion is prompted, and T₀ baseline time. Parameters are fixed scenario assumptions.
results: The illustrative dataset demonstrates the analysis pipeline rather than treatment effectiveness. At mean baseline ability, adaptive friction exceeded ordinary assistance by 7.53 transfer points, with a 95% confidence interval of 5.09–9.97; the static contrast was 6.20 points, with interval 3.76–8.65 (Table 2). Adaptive versus static friction differed by 1.33 points, with interval −1.14–3.79. Consequently, this realisation supports neither a precise learning advantage over static prompts nor a conclusion about real programmers. The favourable arm ordering largely recovers the ordering imposed by the generating coefficients.

The adaptive geometric time ratio was 1.023, with a 90% interval of 0.988–1.060. This interval satisfied both the illustrative upper non-inferiority limit and the stricter descriptive equivalence region. Static friction produced a ratio of 1.290, with interval 1.246–1.336. Adaptive assistance was therefore substantially faster than static prompting within this artificial dataset. Combining the one-sided learning and time bounds yielded a positive joint decision (Figure 1). Such a decision is conditional on the chosen five-point minimum; changing that threshold changes the substantive question, even when the fitted coefficients remain identical.

Ability-dependent estimates revealed why average effects cannot settle personalisation claims. The adaptive transfer contrast was 9.43 points at one standard deviation below mean ability and 5.63 points at one standard deviation above it (Figure 2). Their respective 95% intervals were 6.07–12.79 and 1.87–9.39. These overlapping intervals do not themselves test moderation; that requires the interaction contrast. Delayed adaptive and static advantages over ordinary assistance were 16.39 and 14.67 points. These larger differences follow the explicitly imposed arm-specific decay and cannot be interpreted as evidence that prompts protect long-term memory.

Repeated simulations exposed a substantial difference between detectable improvement and decision readiness. Under source-like assumptions, positive adaptive benefit was detected in every replication at each sample size. Yet the joint criterion passed in only 54.16% of runs with 165 units, compared with 87.04% at 330 and 99.08% at 660 (Table 3). At the smallest size, the Monte Carlo standard error for joint passage was 0.70 percentage points. The illustrative successful dataset therefore understates design uncertainty when considered alone. A convincing-looking single simulation is a poor substitute for operating characteristics.

The original sample-size rationale also proved insufficient for the specified moderator. Interaction rejection under source-like assumptions reached 49.76%, 79.56%, and 98.08% across increasing sample sizes. Thus, 165 units did not deliver approximately eighty-percent moderation power for this generating mechanism. This finding does not establish a universal recruitment target: smaller effects, heavier tails, missing outcomes, model misspecification, or uneven allocation could alter requirements. Across all configurations, transfer-contrast coverage ranged from 94.50% to 95.58%, and absolute bias remained below 0.04 points. These checks support implementation accuracy under the model, not external validity.

Failure scenarios were equally informative (Figure 3). With a two-point adaptive gain, conventional superiority rejection increased from 48.36% to 94.06% as sample size grew, but the joint criterion never passed in 5,000 runs at any size. A large effect accompanied by excessive delay likewise never passed. At the five-point gain boundary, joint passage ranged from 3.70% to 4.94%; at the time boundary it ranged from 2.00% to 4.82%. These frequencies illustrate the conservative behaviour of requiring both conditions, while zero observed passages do not imply a zero underlying probability.

The confidence-bound criterion concerns one candidate policy at mean ability. It does not certify every ability subgroup, guarantee an individual benefit, or prove that the telemetry mechanism caused the simulated arm difference. Subgroup guarantees would require additional estimands and sufficient precision across the intended population. Likewise, the complete-data design omits attrition and task-level dependence, so its sample-size results are conditional benchmarks. For configurations with no observed joint passes, the approximate rule-of-three upper bound is 0.06% per configuration, rather than literal impossibility. Reporting these distinctions matters because simulation precision can be high even when scientific uncertainty about the generating assumptions remains substantial. The next evidential step is therefore an independently evaluated pilot that estimates plausible response magnitudes and interruption costs before any definitive trial recruitment calculation.

The detector analysis identified a complementary mechanism for failure (Figure 4). With need prevalence 0.40, sensitivity 0.80, and specificity 0.85, the assumed response model yielded a 7.50-point expected gain and an 8.2% time increase. Reducing specificity to 0.50 preserved a 7.08-point gain but raised time by 12.4%, violating the budget. False prompts therefore consumed efficiency without necessarily eliminating learning benefit. These are expected values, without inferential uncertainty, and the detector model is separate from the main simulation. Together, the analyses justify evaluating trigger accuracy, meaningful learning, and completion time as distinct quantities before prospective deployment.
conclusion:
Adaptive friction should be evaluated against explicit learning and efficiency requirements rather than a favourable average effect alone. This simulation study formalised that principle through a joint confidence-bound decision and demonstrated its consequences across six generating mechanisms. Under the favourable assumptions, a sample of 165 synthetic users almost always detected some learning benefit but satisfied the stronger joint requirement in only 54.2% of replications. Increasing sample size improved decision reliability and moderation detection, while insufficient benefit or excessive delay remained unacceptable. A separate analytical model showed how false prompts can exhaust the interruption budget even when expected learning gains persist.

These findings establish computational operating characteristics, not the effectiveness of an AI interface. The proposed thresholds, response coefficients, and detector properties require empirical justification. A prospective study should freeze the assistance model, validate telemetry against independent indicators, randomise interface policies, and assess unaided transfer after assistance withdrawal. Delayed testing, accessibility, and missingness should be prespecified. The practical contribution is an auditable standard for deciding what evidence would justify adaptive prompting, together with reproducible calculations that expose the limitations of the initial experimental design.
